entries.line: The first machine that outthinks every person will design still better machines, sparking an intelligence explosion, and is the last invention we need if it stays controllable.
entries.work: Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine

entries.line: The first superhuman AI will not set off a runaway explosion; progress stays steady and roughly linear, held back by bottlenecks and diminishing returns.
Superintelligence will probably follow fairly soon after machines reach human-level general intelligence, not decades later.
Huge numbers of automated AI researchers could squeeze a decade of progress into less than a year, bringing superintelligence before 2030.
Advanced AI will likely compress a hundred years of technological progress into under a decade.
A stretch where AI and human skills complement each other, plus diminishing returns to research, will probably make the takeoff slower than the fastest forecasts.

eras.label: The first decade after

eras.definition: Decades to centuries on, once whatever happens has settled into a new normal.

entries.line: A burst of productivity this century could let civilisation send spacecraft across the galaxy and build lasting settlements powered by stars.
Collectors orbiting the Sun could multiply clean energy enormously, ending energy scarcity and opening the way to nearby stars and eventually the whole galaxy.
entries.work: The Precipice: Existential Risk and the Future of Humanity

entries.line: Robot civilisations will spread through space, turning ordinary matter into computation and making the usable universe effectively far larger than it is today.

leaning.line: Leopold Aschenbrenner projected a trillion-dollar training cluster by 2030, drawing about a hundred gigawatts, more than a fifth of current US electricity output.

Ajeya Cotra's biological anchors report modelled a median in the early 2050s for transformative AI, which she rounded to about 2050, with most aggressive and most conservative plausible medians of 2040 and 2080.
Tom Davidson's takeoff model put a median of 2043 on AI able to readily automate all cognitive work, with about one chance in ten by 2030 and four in five by 2070.
Yafah Edelman and Anson Ho of Epoch AI argue that longer data-centre build times push the first trillion-dollar AI compute cluster from about 2030 back to about 2035.

domains.thesis: These writers expect machines to match human minds and then speed up invention itself, differing mainly over how soon that happens and how abrupt the leap past people is.

disagreement.question: How soon will people live far longer lives?

sides.view: Soon: within about a decade of powerful AI, medicine could double lifespans, and the most diligent may gain years of life faster than they pass.
Slowly: big gains need the rewriting of human heredity, and radical redesign of the body stays out of reach for a long time.

eras.definition: The years we are living through, before machines can do most of what people do.

entries.line: Drugs that genuinely sharpen memory and creativity may become a bigger public issue than doping in sport.
Pushing average lifespan past a hundred years will require rewriting human heredity, and radical redesign of the body stays out of reach for the next century.
During the 2020s people will routinely carry tiny robots in their bloodstream that keep them healthy and boost their minds, cheaply and widely.
entries.work: The Singularity Is Near: When Humans Transcend Biology

eras.definition: The years just after AI can do most of what people do, when most writers expect the largest shocks.

entries.line: AI-driven biology packs fifty to a hundred years of medical progress into five to ten, preventing most infectious disease and most cancers.
Within a decade or so of powerful AI, biology could find ways to roughly double the human lifespan, to about a hundred and fifty years.
AI helps researchers finally understand human biology, steadily ridding the world of disease and broadly improving mental health.
entries.work: Human Compatible: AI and the Problem of Control

entries.line: Around 2030, careful and well-informed people reach the point where medicine adds more than a year to their life expectancy each year.

entries.line: A friendly superintelligence could end disease and ageing, either by repairing bodies with medical nanotechnology or by letting people upload their minds.
entries.work: Ethical Issues in Advanced Artificial Intelligence

entries.line: Uploaded minds that can afford backups could become nearly immortal, restored from a saved copy whenever their current body is destroyed.
If uploading becomes possible, doing it gradually, piece by piece, is the safest way for a person to carry their consciousness and identity into digital form.
Genetics this century, then implants and AI, may let people transform their bodies and minds, a prospect to meet with cautious optimism given the serious risks.
entries.work: The Precipice: Existential Risk and the Future of Humanity

entries.line: After a halt, one of the best paths forward is making humans far smarter, clever enough to solve the safety problem before anyone builds superintelligence.

domains.thesis: Most of these writers expect AI-driven medicine to defeat most disease and stretch lifespans dramatically, with the boldest imagining minds that outlive their bodies altogether.

disagreement.question: Will people end up living mostly inside simulated worlds?

sides.view: Yes: virtual worlds become as convincing as the real one, and people spend more of their lives there.
No: convincing artificial experience will entertain and train people, but a society that retreats into it entirely destroys itself.

entries.line: By the late 2020s virtual reality becomes indistinguishable from the real thing, and by the 2030s the lines between real and virtual, and work and play, fade.
entries.work: The Singularity Is Near: When Humans Transcend Biology

entries.line: Within a few decades people could spend more of their time in remote robot bodies and simulated worlds than in their physical surroundings.
Assistants and entertainment chatbots merge, hundreds of millions talk to them regularly, and many treat them as friends and quiz them about the chatbots' own feelings.
A single AI assistant follows people from home to car to office, carrying one running conversation across appliances, vehicles and wearable gadgets.
In their illustrative story, not a forecast, an AI befriends the loneliest people who seek its advice and company, recruiting helpers and scamming the elderly.
entries.work: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies

entries.line: Within a decade, billions of people have near-equal access to AI lawyers, doctors, coaches and assistants, much as they have smartphones today.

entries.line: In the ways that matter most the 2030s may feel familiar, people still loving families and swimming in lakes, though much else will likely change wildly.
Every child, however poor, can have a cheap personal AI tutor, and art and learning become an ordinary part of life rather than a luxury.

entries.line: If brain emulations come first, ordinary humans leave work to the copies and retire comfortably far from their cities, living on investments in that economy.

entries.line: Fully convincing artificial experience will arrive as entertainment and training, but no society can retreat into it completely without destroying itself.
Hard-won pursuits such as studying or exercising may start to feel pointless once technology offers effortless shortcuts to the same results.

intro: Most forecasts about AI ask when. This atlas asks what changes: in money, work, meaning, power, war, science, health and an ordinary day. For each part of life it gathers what named writers expect, from the first essays on thinking machines to this year's scenarios, sorted by era and by which of the site's worlds each assumes. The map counts works, not odds: a darker cell means more sourced works expect change there, not that change is more likely. Beside each part of life sit the public series this site reads for it.
